concept: PinInput is a row of small recessed windows, one for each digit of a short code. Each window is the same cut-in well as Input, so a code reads as several readings side by side, and the cursor moves from one window to the next as digits arrive.

default_to_avoid.pattern: pin input as a row of bordered boxes with a blinking caret and a hidden single input behind them
default_to_avoid.why_not: The boxes only imitate a field, so selection, paste and screen readers fight the fake; each digit here is a real input in a real window.

default_to_avoid.pattern: pin input cells that turn green or red on every digit as the code is typed
default_to_avoid.why_not: It tells right and wrong by colour alone and spends colour on a label; invalid is a glyph with words under the row.

references.source: Braun ET 66 calculator (Dietrich Lubs, 1987): each figure is read in its own window cut into the body
Braun T 1000 world receiver (Dieter Rams, 1963): the dial scale is read one mark at a time on the inset line
system/FORM.md input class: recessed well, label printed above on the inset line
WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: group with one labelled text input per item

derivation.consequence: the window is recessed into the body (inverse light)
derivation.form: Each cell takes surface.sunken and elevation.well, the same as Input, so a digit reads as cut into the body and never as a key.

derivation.consequence: labels sit on the body's inset line, never floating mid-surface
derivation.form: The label, the row of cells and the message stack in one column, so the label sits on the inset line above the first cell.

derivation.consequence: every part keeps ≥44px hit area even when it draws smaller
derivation.form: Every cell is at least 44px wide and 44px tall, and the row wraps instead of squeezing a cell narrower.

derivation.consequence: every mechanism has its keyboard map
derivation.form: A digit moves to the next cell, Backspace goes back, the arrows, Home and End walk the cells, and a paste fills them all.

derivation.consequence: orange appears once per unit, on the primary control's body only
derivation.form: Digits, edges and the focus ring are ink, and the invalid state is a red glyph with words, never orange.

variants.reason: A reuses the Input window, gives each digit its own 44px target and wraps on a narrow screen; B hides the focused cell inside a joined bar and cannot wrap, and C borrows the LCD face that belongs to displays and prints fake ghost digits that are not in the code.

root.why: The field stacks its label, row of cells and message in one column so the label sits on the inset line above the first cell.

label.why: The printed name uses the label size in medium weight and also names the group of cells for assistive tech.

group.why: The row keeps the cells on one grid step apart and wraps a long code to a second line before it would shrink a cell below 44px.

cell.why: One digit sits in one recessed window with the inverse light, in tabular figures, with a line box tall enough that Thai marks are never cut.

hint.why: The hint is secondary ink on plastic above 4.5:1, printed under the row so it never covers a digit.

error.why: The error message is a red mark with words, never the orange, which stays reserved for the unit's primary control.

glyph.why: A printed mark beside the words means invalid is never told by colour alone, for people who cannot see the red.

md.why: The default cell is 44px square, the smallest target that every part in dial keeps for a finger.

lg.why: A 52px cell with larger figures for the main code of a phone sheet held in one hand.

focus.why: The focused cell shows the same dark ring as every part, and the digit in it is selected so the next key replaces it.

data-filled=true.why: A cell that holds a digit draws its edge in secondary ink, a step darker than the empty cell, so filled and empty differ by outline and not only by the digit.

data-invalid=true.why: An invalid cell draws its edge in the critical red, which is never orange, and the message below names the problem.

data-disabled=true.why: A disabled row loses its recess shadow and fades, so it reads as not taking input right now.

data-readonly=true.why: A read-only row keeps its recess and ink but loses the text cursor, so the code can be read and copied and not changed.

@media forced-colors: active.why: In forced colours each cell keeps a real border and the focus ring uses the system highlight colour.
